title: The pacemaker of the ice ages
teaches: How slow changes in the Earth's orbit time the ice ages, and how the record was read from deep-sea mud

blocks.text: Soon after Agassiz's ice age was accepted, geologists found that it had not been a single event. In the Midwest of the United States and in the Alps, layers of glacial debris were separated by old soils and peat with the remains of warm-climate plants, showing that the ice had advanced, melted away, and advanced again. By the early twentieth century four separate glaciations were recognised in the Alps. The obvious question was why the climate should swing back and forth like this.

In the 1860s and 1870s James Croll, a self-taught Scot who worked as a janitor at a museum in Glasgow and studied in its library, proposed an astronomical answer. The Earth's orbit around the Sun is not fixed. Its shape and its orientation change slowly, through the pull of the other planets, and so does the amount of sunlight reaching each part of the Earth in each season. Croll's version predicted that the last ice age had ended about 80,000 years ago. When geologists showed, from the rate at which waterfalls such as Niagara had retreated, that the ice had left North America only about 10,000 years ago, his theory was dropped.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: There were many glaciations, separated by warm interglacial periods.
Croll suggested that changes in the Earth's orbit cause them, but his timing was wrong.

blocks.text: The idea was revived by Milutin Milanković, a Serbian civil engineer and mathematician. Interned in Budapest as an enemy citizen during the First World War, he spent his time calculating, by hand, how much sunlight each latitude had received in each season over the past several hundred thousand years. He published his curves in 1920 and in 1924 they appeared in a book on ancient climates by Wladimir Köppen and his son-in-law, Alfred Wegener of lesson 8. His full results came out in 1941.

Three things change. The tilt of the Earth's axis wobbles between about 22.1° and 24.5° over about 41,000 years; more tilt means hotter summers and colder winters at high latitudes. The orbit's shape stretches from almost circular to slightly elliptical and back, an eccentricity of between about 0 and 0.06, over roughly 100,000 and 400,000 years. And the timing of the Earth's closest approach to the Sun moves through the seasons over about 21,000 years, a shift called **precession**. Today the Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter; about 11,000 years ago it was closest in July.

Milanković argued that the crucial quantity was the strength of summer at high northern latitudes, around 65° N, where the great ice sheets of North America and Europe began. Winters there are always cold enough for snow. What matters is whether the summer is warm enough to melt it all. A run of weak summers lets snow survive from year to year, and an ice sheet starts to grow.

blocks.caption: Midsummer sunshine at 65° N, averaged over the day, as the tilt, the stretch of the orbit and the timing of the closest approach change. The orbit above is drawn with its stretch exaggerated five times.
blocks.task: Find a combination that gives a cold northern summer, below 445 W/m²

blocks.text: The weakest summers come with low tilt, a stretched orbit, and the Earth at its farthest from the Sun in June. The changes are large: midsummer sunshine at 65° N has varied by about 20% over the last million years, though the total sunlight the Earth receives over a year barely changes at all. The orbit redistributes sunlight between seasons and latitudes rather than adding or removing it.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Tilt varies over about 41,000 years, the orbit's stretch over about 100,000 and 400,000, and the timing of the closest approach over about 21,000.
Milanković proposed that weak summers at high northern latitudes let snow survive and ice sheets grow.
Orbital changes move sunlight between seasons and latitudes; the yearly total for the whole Earth hardly changes.

blocks.text: To test Milanković's idea, geologists needed a continuous record of the ice ages with dates, and the glacial debris on land could not supply one, since each advance of the ice scraped away much of the evidence of the one before. The record came instead from the deep-sea floor, where fine mud and the shells of microscopic plankton settle steadily, a few centimetres every thousand years, undisturbed.

The shells of **foraminifera**, single-celled animals the size of sand grains, are made of calcium carbonate, which contains oxygen. Oxygen comes in two stable isotopes (lesson 7), common oxygen-16 and heavier oxygen-18. Water molecules containing the lighter isotope evaporate a little more readily, so the snow that builds ice sheets is slightly short of oxygen-18. When ice sheets grow, they lock up that light water and leave the oceans slightly richer in oxygen-18, and the foraminifera build their shells from the seawater around them. Measuring the ratio of the two isotopes in shells, layer by layer down a core of sediment, gives a record of how much ice was on land, mixed with a smaller signal from the temperature of the water.

Cesare Emiliani made the first such record in 1955, and Nicholas Shackleton showed in the late 1960s that it mostly measured ice volume. Since then hundreds of cores have been analysed. In 2005 Lorraine Lisiecki and Maureen Raymo combined 57 of them into a single record of the last 5.3 million years, known as the LR04 stack, which the next figure uses.

blocks.caption: The LR04 deep-sea record (Lisiecki and Raymo, 2005): the oxygen isotopes in foraminifera shells, a measure of the ice on land. Up is less ice. A cycle of the chosen length is laid over it, with a score for how well it fits.
blocks.task: Find the length of cycle that best fits the record from 1.2 to 2 million years ago

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Growing ice sheets lock up water rich in oxygen-16, leaving the oceans richer in oxygen-18.
Foraminifera shells in deep-sea sediment record the oxygen isotopes of seawater, and so the volume of ice on land.
The LR04 stack combines 57 such records.

blocks.text: In 1976 James Hays, John Imbrie and Nicholas Shackleton published an analysis of two cores from the southern Indian Ocean, dated using the magnetic reversals of lesson 9. They broke the record of the last 450,000 years into its component cycles, and found three main ones: about 100,000 years, about 42,000 years, and about 23,000 and 19,000 years. These matched the periods of the orbit's stretch, its tilt and its precession. The title of their paper gave this lesson its name: Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages.

The figure shows something the 1976 cores could not. Before about a million years ago, the ice came and went every 41,000 years, in step with the tilt. Over the last 800,000 years the dominant rhythm has been about 100,000 years, with long, slow build-ups of ice ending in rapid melting, a sawtooth pattern. Yet the orbit's stretch, which has a 100,000-year cycle, changes the sunshine reaching 65° N far less than tilt or precession do. Why the longer rhythm took over, and why each long build-up ends in a sudden melt, are still debated. The most likely answers involve the ice sheets themselves, which once they are very large can become unstable, and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which Antarctic ice cores show rising and falling with the ice ages and amplifying the change.

The orbit is the pacemaker, then, but not the whole engine. It sets the timing; the size of the response depends on ice, oceans and the atmosphere. The last glacial maximum was about 21,000 years ago, and the present warm period, the Holocene, began about 11,700 years ago. The ice sheets that left the landscape of the next lesson, and the floods of the ice age branch of this course, belong to the last of these cycles.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The ice-volume record contains cycles of about 100,000, 41,000 and 23,000 to 19,000 years, the periods of the orbital changes.
The 41,000-year rhythm dominated until about a million years ago; the 100,000-year rhythm has dominated since about 800,000 years ago.
The orbit times the ice ages; ice sheets and carbon dioxide amplify the response.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the orbit and the ice ages
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: According to Milanković, what lets an ice sheet start to grow?
choices: Weak summers at high northern latitudes, so the winter's snow does not all melt
Very cold winters at high northern latitudes
A drop in the total sunlight reaching the Earth
items.why: Winters near 65° N are always cold enough for snow. Whether snow builds up year after year depends on summer melting.

items.ask: Which combination gives the weakest northern summers?
choices: Low tilt, a stretched orbit, and the Earth farthest from the Sun in June
High tilt, a circular orbit, and the Earth closest to the Sun in June
High tilt and a stretched orbit, with the Earth closest to the Sun in June
items.why: Low tilt weakens all high-latitude summers; a stretched orbit with the far point in June makes June sunlight weaker still.

items.ask: Why does seawater become richer in oxygen-18 when ice sheets grow?
choices: Water with lighter oxygen-16 evaporates more easily, so ice sheets lock up light water and leave the heavy behind
Ice sheets release oxygen-18 into the sea as they grow
Cold water absorbs oxygen-18 from the air
items.why: Snow on ice sheets is short of oxygen-18. Storing it on land leaves the oceans, and the shells grown in them, slightly enriched in oxygen-18.

items.ask: The deep-sea record shows a strong 41,000-year cycle from 1.2 to 2 million years ago. Which part of the orbit has that period?
choices: The timing of the closest approach to the Sun
items.why: The tilt varies between about 22.1° and 24.5° over about 41,000 years.

items.ask: What is puzzling about the 100,000-year rhythm of the last 800,000 years?
choices: The orbital cycle with that period changes summer sunshine much less than tilt or precession do
No orbital change has a period anywhere near 100,000 years
It is too regular to be caused by the orbit
items.why: Eccentricity does vary over about 100,000 years, but its direct effect on summer sunshine is small, so ice sheets and carbon dioxide must amplify it.

learned: Slow changes in the Earth's tilt, the stretch of its orbit and the timing of its closest approach to the Sun change summer sunshine at high latitudes.
Weak northern summers let snow survive and ice sheets grow.
Oxygen isotopes in foraminifera shells from deep-sea mud record the volume of ice on land.
The ice ages follow the orbital cycles: 41,000 years until about a million years ago, 100,000 years since, amplified by ice sheets and carbon dioxide.
